title: Biosphere 2: the sealed world where the oxygen ran out

slides.text: Biosphere 2 was a $150 million, three-acre glass and steel miniature Earth in the Arizona desert. The goal: prove humans could live inside a sealed ecosystem.

image.credit: Photo: Daniel Oberhaus / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

slides.text: On September 26, 1991, four men and four women walked in and the doors were sealed. The plan was two years with no fresh air from outside.
But the oxygen kept falling, from about 21% to about 14%. The crew said it felt like living at 14,000 feet.

image.credit: Photo: Daniel Oberhaus / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

slides.text: Ants and cockroaches exploded in number. Hummingbirds died. The crew worked long days on small meals and lost serious weight.
The cause puzzled everyone. Later work pointed to microbes in the rich soil eating oxygen, and a cloudy year that slowed plant growth.

image.credit: Photo: Jesuiseduardo / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

slides.text: Outside air was added to keep the crew safe, which drew criticism for a project billed as sealed. They still stayed the full two years, stepping out on September 26, 1993.
Today the University of Arizona runs Biosphere 2 as a research center.

caption:
Eight people locked themselves inside a glass building in the desert, and then the air started running out.

Biosphere 2, a three-acre, $150 million glass and steel structure near Tucson, Arizona, was built as a miniature Earth to test whether people could live in a sealed ecosystem. On September 26, 1991, four men and four women entered for a planned two-year stay.

Things went differently than planned. Oxygen fell from about 21% to about 14%, which the crew compared to living at 14,000 feet. Ants and cockroaches multiplied, hummingbirds died, and the crew lost weight on long workdays and small meals.

The cause was a puzzle at first. Later research pointed to microbes in the organic-rich soil using up oxygen, with cloudy weather limiting plant photosynthesis. Outside oxygen was eventually added to keep everyone safe, which drew criticism because the project had been billed as a closed system.

The crew still finished, walking out on September 26, 1993. The University of Arizona now runs the site as a research center.
